problem: Find the minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{3}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Minimum Value Given a Canonical Form on the Unit Sphere
examples.problem: Find the minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x})=5x_1^2 - 4x_2^2 - 6x_3^2$ given that $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1.$
examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that $x_1^2 \geq 0$ and $x_2^2 \geq 0.$ So, we have that

$$
5x_1^2 \geq -6x_1^2, \qquad -4x_2^2 \geq -6x_2^2.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =5{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2}-6{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & \ge -6{x}_{1}^{2}-6{x}_{2}^{2}-6{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =-6({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $\| \mathbf{x} \| = 1$ is equivalent to $x_1^2 + x_2^2 + x_3^2 =1.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-6({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2})=-6(1)=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(\mathbf{x}) \geq -6.$

So, the value of $Q(\mathbf{x})$ can be no smaller than $-6.$ But before we conclude that $-6$ is the minimum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(\mathbf{x}) = -6.$

Notice that when ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14070559/assets/d509eb79bc8d9a96b60922166e49d0225eac7a99d2614859c31af15199d4d47c.png) we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =5{x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2}-6{x}_{3}^{2} \\  & =5(0)^{2}-4(0)^{2}-6(1)^{2} \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $\| \mathbf{x} \| =1,$ the minimum value of $Q(\mathbf{x})$ is equal to $-6.$

feedback.problem: Find the maximum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2}$ given that $‖x‖=1.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${x}_{2}^{2}\ge 0.$ So, we have that

$$
2{x}_{2}^{2}\le 4{x}_{2}^{2}.
$$

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & \le 4{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that $‖x‖=1$ is equivalent to ${x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=1.$ So, 

$$
\begin{aligned}4({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2})=4(1)=4.\end{aligned}
$$

and, in turn, $Q(x)\le 4.$

So, the value of $Q(x)$ can be no greater than $4.$ But before we conclude that $4$ is the maximum, we need to find a vector such that $Q(x)=4.$

Notice that when  $x={[\begin{aligned}1 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{T},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x) & =4{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{2}^{2} \\  & =4(1)^{2}+2(0)^{2} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, given that $‖x‖=1,$ the maximum value of $Q(x)$ is equal to $4.$
